passage:
Diary, Monday.
Our class has a book shelf with no lock. Rule: take one, leave one, write your name in the register. Today I saw Minakshi take two comics and leave none. I almost said nothing, since she's my friend. But if everyone did that, the shelf would be empty in a week, and Ma'am trusted us enough not to lock it. So at break I told her quietly. "Sorry, Nilesh," she said. "I forgot to bring one." Tomorrow she'll bring two. I'm glad I said it. It's not about Ma'am catching us. It's about all of us keeping it working.

qa.q: What is the rule for the class book shelf?
qa.a: Take one, leave one, and write your name in the register.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh almost say nothing?
qa.a: Nilesh didn't want to trouble a friend, but also felt the shelf only works if everyone keeps the rule.

qa.q: What did Nilesh's quiet approach get right?
qa.a: Nilesh spoke privately, which let Minakshi fix it without being shamed, and kept the trust-based rule alive.

qa.q: How might Ma'am feel if she heard about this?
qa.a: Pleased that the class is keeping the system fair on its own, showing her trust was well placed.

grounding: It shows a child upholding a shared rule because the system depends on everyone's trust, not on being caught.

passage: At the village hand pump, the rule was simple: one bucket each, then back of the line. Nobody enforced it; it worked because everyone did it. Jasleen, eleven, was fourth in line when her cousin Amandeep ran up. "Let me go before you, just this once. Mummy's shouting." Jasleen looked at the three women behind her, their buckets waiting. "If I let you, they'll let their cousins, and nobody gets water on time." Then she added, "Stand behind me, and I'll help you carry yours after." Amandeep sighed, but got in line.

qa.q: What is the rule at the hand pump?
qa.a: One bucket each, then back of the line.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen look at the women behind her before answering?
qa.a: She was concerned about fairness to them, knowing the line only works if everyone keeps to it.

qa.q: What made Jasleen's answer both fair and kind?
qa.a: She kept the rule but offered to help carry Amandeep's bucket, so Amandeep wasn't simply turned away.

qa.q: What would change if Jasleen had let Amandeep skip?
qa.a: Others might start letting their relatives in too, and the trust that keeps the line working could break down.

grounding: It shows a girl keeping a shared queue rule because it rests on everyone's mutual trust.

passage: In their school in Accra, the rule on the veranda was that bags stayed open on the bench during football, and nobody touched anyone else's. After the game Kofi, twelve, found a folded cedi note on the floor beside Nadia's bag. Some boys said, "Finders keepers." Kofi shook his head. "Last month she found my watch and gave it back. If we start taking stuff, we'll all have to carry our bags onto the pitch." He handed Nadia the note. She said, "I owe you a mango." He laughed. "You owe me nothing. That's the deal."

qa.q: What did Kofi find beside Nadia's bag?
qa.a: A folded cedi note.

qa.q: Why did Kofi think of the watch Nadia had returned?
qa.a: He felt that trust works both ways, and since she had been honest with him, he wanted to be honest with her.

qa.q: How could Kofi respond if the boys keep saying "finders keepers"?
qa.a: Explain simply that the bench only stays safe if everyone returns things, as he just did.

qa.q: How does Nadia see Kofi returning the money?
qa.a: She is grateful and wants to repay him, showing the give-and-take that keeps their trust going.

grounding: It shows a boy keeping an unwritten rule out of reciprocity and the trust it protects.

passage: At the school canteen, Manjula Aunty gave Ritu change for her samosa. Walking back, Ritu counted: ten rupees too much. Her friend said, 'Keep it, she won't notice.' Ritu stopped. 'She trusts us. If we all kept extra, she'd lose money, and then she'd stop letting us pay later when we forget cash.' She went back. 'Aunty, you gave me extra.' Manjula smiled. 'Thank you, Ritu. You can pay tomorrow anytime you're short.'

qa.q: How much extra change did Ritu get?
qa.a: She got ten rupees too much.

qa.q: Why did Ritu decide to return the money?
qa.a: She thought about fairness and trust, realising that keeping it would hurt Aunty and break the trust between them.

qa.q: What does Ritu's choice show about following rules?
qa.a: It shows following fair rules can keep trust going both ways, which benefits everyone.

qa.q: How might Manjula Aunty see Ritu after this?
qa.a: She will likely trust Ritu more and be even more willing to help her. 😊

grounding: Illustrates a child internalising fairness and rule-following based on mutual trust at a school canteen.

passage: I watch Suraj and Ojas play cricket in the lane from my window every evening. Yesterday Ojas hit the ball into Mrs. Mehta's garden. They'd agreed that was out. Ojas said, 'But it was a great shot!' Suraj shook his head. 'We said garden is out. If we change it now, why have rules?' Ojas frowned but handed over the bat. Later, Suraj was out the same way, and he gave the bat back without arguing. They're younger than me, but they're fairer than most grown-ups.

qa.q: Where did Ojas hit the ball?
qa.a: Ojas hit it into Mrs. Mehta's garden.

qa.q: What does Ojas frowning but handing over the bat suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Ojas felt disappointed but accepted the rule because they had both agreed to it.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Suraj following the same rule when he got out showed fairness, which kept their trust and the game going.

qa.q: How does the narrator see Suraj and Ojas?
qa.a: The narrator admires them, seeing them as fairer than most grown-ups.

grounding: Shows children following agreed rules out of mutual fairness and trust, observed by a neighbour.
